Upper bounds — holds for every partial

  • \(\mathrm{ndeg}(f) \le \mathrm{C}^1(f)\)
    Sum the certificates. For each minimal $1$-certificate $C$ let $\mathbb{1}_C(x) = \prod_{i \in C} \tfrac{1 + (2c_i-1)(2x_i-1)}{2}$, of degree $|C| \le \mathrm{C}^1(f)$, and put $p = \sum_C \mathbb{1}_C$. Every term is $0$ or $1$, so on the domain $p(x) > 0$ exactly when $x$ is consistent with some $1$-certificate -- that is, exactly when $f(x) = 1$.

Lower bounds / separations — there is a family achieving this

  • \(\mathrm{ndeg}(\wedge_n) = \mathrm{C}^1(\wedge_n) = n\)
    witness: \(\mathrm{AND}_n\)

Incomparable to $\mathrm{ndeg} \le \deg$ and often much sharper: \(\mathrm{OR}_n\) has $\mathrm{C}^1 = \mathrm{ndeg} = 1$ against $\deg = n$, while \(\mathrm{MP}_m\) has $\mathrm{C}^1 = \mathrm{ndeg} = m$ against $\deg = m^3$. Both bounds are needed for the closure to see the smaller of the two.

see also: \(\mathrm{ndeg}(f)\), \(\mathrm{C}^1(f)\), \(\mathrm{NQ}(f)\), \(\deg(f)\), \(\mathrm{OR}_n\), \(\mathrm{MP}_m\) data/relations/13-definitional.yaml

up.note: An exact characterisation, not merely a polynomial relation: nondeterministic quantum query complexity is half the nondeterministic degree. The acceptance amplitude of a $T$-query algorithm is a degree-$2T$ polynomial nonzero exactly on the $1$-inputs, and conversely $p$ may be rescaled by its maximum over the cube; nonvanishing is scale-invariant and off-domain behaviour is unconstrained either way, so this is a statement about partial functions.

Upper bounds — holds for every partial

  • \(\mathrm{ndeg}(f) \le \deg(f)\)
    A representing polynomial is a nondeterministic one. If $p$ agrees with $f$ on $\mathrm{Dom}(f)$ then, $f$ being $\{0,1\}$-valued, $p(x) \ne 0$ exactly when $f(x) = 1$ there. Both measures constrain the domain only, so the promise costs nothing.

Lower bounds / separations — there is a family achieving this

  • \(\mathrm{ndeg}(\wedge_n) = \deg(\wedge_n) = n\)
    witness: \(\mathrm{AND}_n\)
    Tight: $\prod_i x_i$ is the only multilinear polynomial vanishing off $1^n$, up to scale.

The reverse fails as badly as possible -- \(\mathrm{OR}_n\) has $\mathrm{ndeg} = 1$ and $\deg = n$ -- so nothing is bounded in terms of $\mathrm{ndeg}$, and the $\mathrm{ndeg}$ column is a column of $\infty$. That asymmetry is the measure's whole character: a nondeterministic degree only has to be nonzero, and "nonzero" is a single linear condition away for any function with a one-bit certificate.

see also: \(\mathrm{ndeg}(f)\), \(\deg(f)\), \(\mathrm{NQ}(f)\), \(\mathrm{rdeg}(f)\), \(\mathrm{AND}_n\), \(\mathrm{OR}_n\) data/relations/13-definitional.yaml

up.note: Take the numerator. If $p/q = f$ on $\mathrm{Dom}(f)$ then, $f$ being $\{0,1\}$-valued, $f(x) = 1 \iff p(x) \ne 0$ there, so $\mathrm{ndeg}(f) \le \deg p \le \mathrm{rdeg}(f)$; running the same argument on $p - q$, which vanishes exactly on $f^{-1}(1)$, gives $\mathrm{ndeg}(\bar f) \le \mathrm{rdeg}(f)$. Those two are the easy half of the characterisation $\mathrm{rdeg}(f) = \max\{\mathrm{ndeg}(f), \mathrm{ndeg}(\bar f)\}$ quoted at \(\mathrm{rdeg}(f)\).

Upper bounds — holds for every partial

  • \(\mathrm{ndeg}(f) \le \mathrm{rdeg}(f)\)
    deWolf03 MahadevdeWolf15
    Take the numerator. If $p/q = f$ on $\mathrm{Dom}(f)$ then, $f$ being $\{0,1\}$-valued, $f(x) = 1 \iff p(x) \ne 0$ there, so $\mathrm{ndeg}(f) \le \deg p \le \mathrm{rdeg}(f)$; running the same argument on $p - q$, which vanishes exactly on $f^{-1}(1)$, gives $\mathrm{ndeg}(\bar f) \le \mathrm{rdeg}(f)$. Those two are the easy half of the characterisation $\mathrm{rdeg}(f) = \max\{\mathrm{ndeg}(f), \mathrm{ndeg}(\bar f)\}$ quoted at \(\mathrm{rdeg}(f)\).

Lower bounds / separations — there is a family achieving this

  • \(\mathrm{ndeg}(\wedge_n) = \mathrm{rdeg}(\wedge_n) = n\)
    witness: \(\mathrm{AND}_n\)
    Tight whenever the harder of the two sides is the function's own: $\mathrm{ndeg}(\overline{\wedge_n}) = 1$.

So $\mathrm{ndeg}$ is the one-sided half of $\mathrm{rdeg}$, and an upper bound in terms of $\mathrm{ndeg}$ is strictly the stronger statement -- which is why the $\mathrm{rdeg}$ column is full of open cells (is $\mathrm{D}$ polynomially bounded by $\mathrm{rdeg}$?) while the $\mathrm{ndeg}$ column is full of closed ones: \(\mathrm{OR}_n\) settles every cell there in the negative at once.

see also: \(\mathrm{ndeg}(f)\), \(\mathrm{rdeg}(f)\), \(\mathrm{NQ}(f)\), \(\mathrm{rdeg}_{\varepsilon}(f)\), \(\mathrm{AND}_n\), \(\mathrm{OR}_n\) data/relations/13-definitional.yaml
